children.text: A risk register is a list. A portfolio manager needs to see a shape: which risks cluster, which share a cause, which would trigger others, and which are scored modestly but still demand action now. Chapter 15 makes that shift by plotting the register by probability and impact, and by reading it against the dependency logic of the whole book.

This lesson reads Vermont's register the way the book does: as a heat map, as a set of risks with shared causes, and as a set of signals that should trigger escalation. It then shows how the platform's simulators turn the register's two Technology risks into something you can watch happen.
The aim is to move from asking how big each risk is to asking what the risks together say about where the portfolio is fragile.
The Heat Map

Figure 15.7 plots each risk on a grid, probability on one axis and impact on the other. The book's comment is that the register's shape is clearer than its rows. The two risks scored 20 share the critical corner of the map, high probability and critical impact, and one of them is the absence of the portfolio function itself.

That observation carries the chapter's whole argument. The single most dangerous condition in the portfolio is not a technical failure or a budget shortfall. It is the lack of anyone positioned to manage the other risks. A register whose top risk is 'nobody is managing this register' is telling its readers what to do first.

The map also shows what sits in the middle. Social-risk adjustment (R-08) scores 12, mid-map. The book's reminder is that a moderate score is not a licence to wait: the sequencing test says this component has no upstream blocker and should already be running. Risk score and dependency status answer different questions, and the portfolio manager needs both.

Risk score tells you how bad a risk would be. Dependency status tells you whether the work that prevents it can start now. A moderate risk whose prevention is unblocked deserves action before a severe risk whose prevention must wait.
Shared Causes and Correlated Risks

Risks on a register are often treated as independent, but in a five-pillar portfolio many share a cause. R-01, the analytics vendor not being operational, and R-06, persistent VITL connectivity gaps, are both failures of the Technology pillar. If Technology slips, both are likely to materialize together, and through the dependency chain they then degrade Economics and Clinical work at the same time.

Correlation changes how risks should be managed. Two risks that would each be survivable alone can be overwhelming together. A portfolio manager who mitigates R-01 and R-06 separately, with different owners and no shared plan, may miss that the most effective mitigation for both is the same: protecting and resourcing the Technology program as a whole.

Capacity risks correlate too. R-03, an overcommitted agency producing a non-binding Strategic Plan, and R-10, no portfolio infrastructure, both stem from the same shortage of management capacity. The book's response to R-03 includes establishing the portfolio office, the same action that avoids R-10. One well-chosen response can retire several risks.

Correlation also runs through external risks. Federal Medicaid cuts (R-05) and the loss of the EAST Fund backstop after the AHEAD withdrawal hit the same Clinical and Economics components at once. Scenario planning that assumes both happen together is more honest than planning for each separately and hoping they do not coincide.

children.text: Watching a Risk Happen in the Simulators

Chapter 15's platform guide suggests a direct way to see why the Technology risks dominate. Open the HTR Simulator at /htr-simulator, load the Vermont, Fall 2026 scenario, and lower the Technology score. Economics and Clinical fall with it. The book calls this the risk register's R-01 and R-06 in visual form.

The effect comes from how the simulator models dependency. Each pillar is gated on the delivered strength of the pillars upstream of it, not on their nominal scores, so a weaker Technology pillar caps Economics, and the capped Economics in turn caps Clinical. A risk that materializes in one pillar propagates down the chain, which is exactly why cross-pillar risks belong on the portfolio register.

The Impact Simulation at /impact-simulation lets you model what a single component slipping does to the rest of the portfolio, and shows which components have no slack: the ones whose slip moves other pillars' outcomes. Together the two tools turn an abstract score into a visible consequence, which is often what a governance body needs before it will fund a mitigation.

children.text: When to Escalate

Escalation is a response in its own right: referring a risk to a higher level when it exceeds the current owner's authority. In a portfolio, escalation paths follow the governance tiers from Track 2. A component lead escalates to the pillar program manager, the program manager to the Portfolio Manager, and the Portfolio Manager to the governance body, which for Vermont is the AHS Secretary with the HCAC and the Green Mountain Care Board.

Good escalation is triggered by rules agreed in advance, not by frustration. Typical triggers are a score crossing a threshold, a risk spanning pillars owned by different program managers, a response that needs resources the owner does not control, and a risk to a component on the portfolio's true critical path. Writing these triggers down protects owners from being blamed for escalating and protects the governance body from surprises.

R-10 shows the limit of escalation. Its owner in the register is the AHS Secretary, the top of the structure, because the risk concerns whether the structure exists at all. When the highest-scored risk is owned at the top, the governance body cannot delegate it; it has to act.

Escalation should also flow downward. When the governance body decides on an escalated risk, the decision and its reasoning need to return to the people who raised it, so the same risk is not escalated again next month and so owners learn what the governance body will and will not decide.

body.message: Escalating a risk moves the decision to someone with more authority. It does not remove the original owner's responsibility to supply the analysis, the options and the consequences of inaction. An escalation without those is just a complaint.
body.title: Escalation is not abdication

children.text: A Monthly Reading Routine

Each month, before the governance review, the portfolio office should read the register in three passes. First, the heat map: what has moved toward the critical corner, and why? Second, shared causes: which risks have the same root, and is there a single response that addresses several? Third, dependency status: which risks can be reduced by work that is unblocked today, regardless of score?

The output is short: the two or three risks that need a decision from the governance body this month, with options and consequences. That is what turns a register from a compliance artifact into the main agenda of portfolio governance.

Keep a record of how each month's top risks were handled. Over a year, that record is evidence for federal partners, legislators and auditors that the portfolio was actively managed, which is itself one of the benefits the book claims for a portfolio office.
The register's best monthly output is not the full table. It is two or three decisions the governance body must make now, each with options and the cost of not deciding.

points: Plotting the register by probability and impact reveals its shape; Vermont's two risks scored 20 share the critical corner.
One of the two top risks is the absence of the portfolio function itself, which tells readers what to do first.
A moderate score is not a licence to wait: social-risk adjustment scores 12 but has no upstream blocker and should already be running.
Many portfolio risks share causes; R-01 and R-06 are both Technology failures, and R-03 and R-10 both stem from missing management capacity.
Lowering Technology in the HTR Simulator shows R-01 and R-06 propagating to Economics and Clinical, because each pillar is gated on delivered upstream strength.
Escalation should follow the governance tiers and pre-agreed triggers, and must carry analysis, options and consequences.
A monthly three-pass reading (heat map, shared causes, dependency status) produces the two or three decisions governance must make.

body.explanation: Risks with a shared cause are likely to materialize together and, through the dependency chain, to degrade Economics and Clinical at the same time. Managing them separately can miss that the most effective response is common to both. Reading the register by shared cause makes that response visible.

Recognize the shared cause: protecting and resourcing the Technology program as a whole may mitigate both
Accept both, since Technology risks are outside the portfolio's control
